blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
With a view to facilitating the scaling up of access to antiretroviral therapy, and in line with a 
public health approach, this publication outlines recent revisions WHO has made to case 
definitions for surveillance of HIV and the clinical and the immunological classification for HIV-
related disease. HIV case definitions are defined and harmonized with the clinical staging and 
immunological classifications to facilitate improved HIV-related surveillance, to better track the 
incidence, prevalence and treatment burden of HIV infection and to plan appropriate public 
health responses. The r

summary.text: The introduction explains that WHO revised its HIV case definitions for surveillance and harmonized them with clinical staging and immunological classification, to support scaling up antiretroviral therapy and track the HIV epidemic. It notes the revisions came from regional consultations in 2004–2005 and a consensus meeting in 2006, and that AIDS reporting alone no longer gives reliable data now that treatment delays AIDS.

summary.text: Traces the history of WHO's AIDS case definitions from the 1985 Bangui definition through revisions in 1986, 1989 and 1994, noting weak performance of the paediatric definition. It explains that AIDS reporting in low- and middle-income countries has been incomplete, while treatment has reduced new AIDS cases and deaths where coverage is high.

blocks.title: Surveillance and case reporting for HIV
blocks.content:
HIV counselling and testing has led to an increase in the numbers of adults and children being 
tested and diagnosed with HIV infection. Accurate data are needed on adults and children 
diagnosed with HIV infection to facilitate estimation of the treatment and care burden, to plan for 
effective prevention and care interventions and assess care interventions. WHO therefore 
recommends that countries consider conducting reporting of newly diagnosed cases of HIV 
infection in adults and children (Box 1). The requirements for the confidentiality and security of 
HIV surveillance data are the same

summary.text: Recommends that countries report newly diagnosed HIV infection in adults and children, with the same confidentiality as AIDS reporting and with providers initiating reports. It also sets the age definitions used for children, adults, youth and infants.

blocks.title: WHO case definition for HIV infection
blocks.content:
To facilitate the reporting of HIV infection, WHO recommends the following:
HIV cases diagnosed and not previously reported in each country should be reported according 
to a standard national case definition. A case of HIV infection is defined as an individual with HIV 
infection irrespective of clinical stage (including severe or stage 4 clinical disease, also known 
as AIDS) confirmed by laboratory criteria according to country definitions and requirements. 
Countries should develop and regularly review their testing algorithms for diagnostic and 
surveillance purposes. WHO provides a simp

summary.text: Sets out WHO's recommendation that new HIV cases be reported using a standard national case definition confirmed by laboratory criteria at any clinical stage. Box 1 gives the diagnostic criteria, using two antibody tests or virological tests for people aged 18 months or older and virological tests for younger children because maternal antibodies persist.

summary.text: Defines advanced HIV infection, including AIDS, for reporting, based on stage 3 or 4 clinical conditions or CD4 thresholds by age. A footnote gives the stricter definition of AIDS, and the text states that separate AIDS case reporting is no longer required where HIV and advanced HIV are reported.

blocks.title: Primary HIV infection
blocks.content:
where recognized and documented, is useful and should be encouraged. The United States 
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) are expected to develop a case definition for 
reporting primary HIV infection. Primary HIV infection can be recognized in infants, children, 
adolescents and adults; it can be asymptomatic or be associated with features of an acute 
retroviral syndrome of variable severity [16-21]. Primary infection usually presents as an acute 
febrile illness 2–4 weeks postexposure, often with lymphadenopathy, pharyngitis, maculopapular 
rash, orogenital ulcers and meningo

summary.text: Describes primary HIV infection, which may be silent or cause an acute febrile illness with rash, sore throat and swollen glands a few weeks after exposure, and how it can be identified. It reviews the history of WHO clinical staging, explains that the new staging is harmonized across ages, and proposes using new or recurrent staging events to assess people on antiretroviral therapy.

Treatment with potent and effective antiretroviral therapy regimens can reverse and improve

summary.text: Gives the four WHO clinical stages from asymptomatic to severe and explains how staging events can guide decisions for people on antiretroviral therapy after 24 weeks, when early events may reflect immune reconstitution. It describes CD4 cell counts and percentages as the standard measure of HIV-related immune deficiency. It notes that healthy infants have much higher CD4 values than adults, which fall with age.

summary.text: An annex table giving clinical and definitive criteria for diagnosing each HIV staging event in adults and in children under 15 years. Entries range from oral ulceration, skin conditions and fungal nail infections to severe weight loss, chronic diarrhoea and oesophageal candidiasis. Stage 4 conditions such as extrapulmonary tuberculosis and visceral herpes are also covered. The end covers disseminated fungal and mycobacterial infections, which need laboratory confirmation.

summary.text: Annex 2 sets out criteria for a presumptive diagnosis of severe HIV disease in HIV antibody-positive infants under 18 months, based on AIDS-indicator conditions or a combination of thrush, severe pneumonia and severe sepsis. It notes supporting factors such as maternal death or low CD4 and urges confirmation as soon as possible.
